SECTION 1: FOUNDATIONAL STATISTICS & PROBABILITY

1.1 Descriptive vs. Inferential Statistics

Descriptive statistics summarize the sample you actually have. They make no claims beyond it.

Category Measures
Central tendency Mean, median, mode, trimmed mean
Dispersion Variance, standard deviation, IQR, range, MAD
Shape Skewness (asymmetry), kurtosis (tail heaviness)
Association Covariance, Pearson (linear), Spearman (monotonic, rank-based)

Inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a population. The main tools are point estimates, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and regression inference.

Sample variance uses Bessel's correction, which makes it an unbiased estimator of the population variance:

Standard deviation vs. standard error. Standard deviation measures how spread out individual data points are. Standard error measures how spread out a statistic (such as the mean) would be across repeated samples:

Central Limit Theorem (CLT). For i.i.d. variables with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal as the sample grows, whatever the shape of the population:

⚠️ Interview gotchas

  • Confidence interval interpretation: A 95% CI does not mean "there is a 95% probability the true parameter is in this interval." It means the procedure captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. (A Bayesian credible interval does support the probability statement.)
  • Skewed data (e.g., revenue, latency): The mean is pulled by the tail. Report the median or a trimmed mean, or use a log transform.
  • The CLT applies to the sampling distribution of the mean, not to the raw data. It also converges slowly for heavy-tailed data, and it fails when variance is infinite (e.g., Cauchy, some Pareto distributions).
  • Pearson r = 0 does not mean independence. It only rules out a linear relationship (for example, y = x² on a symmetric range has r ≈ 0).

1.2 Probability Distributions

Normal (Gaussian)

  • Empirical rule: about 68% / 95% / 99.7% of values fall within 1 / 2 / 3 σ of the mean.
  • DS use cases: sampling distributions of means (the basis of z-tests and t-tests), regression residuals, measurement error, the noise assumption in Gaussian processes.
  • Gotcha: Most real business metrics (revenue, session length) are not normal. Their means become approximately normal at large n.

Binomial

The number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with success probability p:

  • DS use cases: conversion counts in A/B tests, click-throughs out of impressions, defective units in a batch.
  • Normal approximation is valid when and .

Poisson

The count of events in a fixed interval at a constant rate λ, with events independent of each other:

  • DS use cases: support tickets per hour, website visits per minute, defects per unit, insurance claims.
  • Binomial approximation: When n is large and p is small, Binomial(n, p) ≈ Poisson(λ = np).
  • Gotcha (overdispersion): Real count data often has variance greater than the mean. In that case, use a Negative Binomial or quasi-Poisson model.

Exponential

The waiting time between events in a Poisson process:

  • Memoryless property:
  • DS use cases: time between customer arrivals, time-to-failure (simple reliability and survival models), queueing models.
  • Gotcha: Real failure rates usually change over time (wear-out or infant mortality). Use Weibull or Cox models when the hazard is not constant.
Distribution Type Parameters Mean Variance Typical DS question
Normal Continuous μ, σ μ σ² "Is the mean difference significant?"
Binomial Discrete n, p np np(1−p) "Did conversion rate change?"
Poisson Discrete λ λ λ "Are tickets/hour abnormally high?"
Exponential Continuous λ 1/λ 1/λ² "Expected time until next event?"

1.3 Hypothesis Testing

Framework:

  1. State the null hypothesis (no effect) and the alternative .
  2. Choose a significance level α (commonly 0.05).
  3. Compute a test statistic, e.g., the t-statistic:
  4. Compute the p-value and compare it to α.

p-value: The probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what was observed, assuming H₀ is true:

H₀ True H₀ False
Reject H₀ Type I error (False Positive), probability = α Correct, probability = Power = 1 − β
Fail to reject H₀ Correct, probability = 1 − α Type II error (False Negative), probability = β
  • α (significance level): The false positive rate you accept.
  • β: The probability of missing a real effect.
  • Power (1 − β): The probability of detecting a real effect. The usual target is 0.8.

What increases power:

  • A larger sample size n
  • A larger true effect size
  • Lower variance (achieved through variance reduction, stratification, or CUPED)
  • A higher α (at the cost of more false positives)
  • A one-sided test (only when you can justify it in advance)

Multiple testing: With m independent tests, the probability of at least one false positive is .

  • Bonferroni: Use α/m. This controls the family-wise error rate (FWER) and is conservative.
  • Benjamini–Hochberg: Controls the false discovery rate (FDR). It is less conservative and is the default choice when screening many metrics.

⚠️ Interview gotchas

  • A p-value is not P(H₀ is true | data), and it is not the size of the effect.
  • "Fail to reject" ≠ "accept H₀." Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, especially in an underpowered test.
  • With very large n, trivially small effects become statistically significant. Always report the effect size and its CI, and judge practical significance separately.
  • Use Welch's t-test by default. It does not assume equal variances.

1.4 A/B Testing

Sample size

For two proportions (two-sided test), the sample size per group is:

For continuous metrics:

Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE)

The MDE is the smallest true effect the test can reliably detect at the chosen α and power. Rearranging the formula above:

Key relationship: Required sample size scales with 1/MDE². Halving the MDE needs about 4× the traffic.

pythonfrom statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

# Baseline 10% conversion, want to detect lift to 11% (10% relative MDE)
es = proportion_effectsize(0.11, 0.10)          # Cohen's h
n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=es, alpha=0.05, power=0.8,
                                 ratio=1.0, alternative='two-sided')
print(f"Required per group: {int(n):,}")         # ~14,700 per arm

Variance reduction with CUPED

CUPED uses a pre-experiment covariate X (e.g., the same metric measured before the test) to remove explainable variance from the outcome Y:

Variance falls by a factor of , where ρ is the correlation between X and Y. This can shorten experiments substantially.

Common pitfalls

Pitfall What goes wrong Mitigation
Peeking / optional stopping Checking p-values repeatedly inflates the Type I error far above α Fix the sample size up front, or use sequential tests (O'Brien-Fleming, mSPRT, always-valid p-values)
Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) The observed split differs from the design (e.g., 50.8/49.2) because of a randomization or logging bug Run a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. If SRM is present, do not trust the results
Novelty / primacy effects Users react to the change itself, not its lasting value Run longer and analyze effects by cohort over time
Network effects / interference (SUTVA violation) Treatment users affect control users (marketplaces, social products) Cluster randomization, geo-experiments, switchback designs
Unit of randomization ≠ unit of analysis Randomizing by user but analyzing per session understates variance Delta method or cluster-robust SEs
Multiple metrics / segments Fishing for significance across many slices Pre-register a primary metric and apply FDR control
Day-of-week / seasonality Incomplete weekly cycles bias results Run in full-week multiples (minimum 1–2 weeks)
Simpson's paradox Traffic mix changes during the test and reverses the aggregate result Stratify, keep allocation constant
Twyman's Law Any result that looks too good is probably a bug Audit the instrumentation

⚠️ Gotcha: "The test was significant on day 3, so we stopped early." This is a red flag. Under continuous peeking, the real false positive rate can exceed 20–30%.

SECTION 2: RIGOROUS DATA PREPARATION & IMPUTATION

2.1 Missing Data Mechanisms

Let R be the missingness indicator, the observed data, and the missing data.

Mechanism Formal definition Example Consequence
MCAR (Missing Completely at Random) A sensor randomly drops packets Complete-case analysis is unbiased but loses power
MAR (Missing at Random) Younger users skip the income field (age is observed) Model-based imputation (MICE) gives unbiased estimates
MNAR (Missing Not at Random) depends on High earners hide income because it is high No standard imputation is unbiased. Requires domain modeling, selection models (Heckman) or sensitivity analysis

Diagnostics:

  • Little's MCAR test checks whether data is MCAR.
  • You can also compare feature distributions for missing vs. non-missing rows, or train a classifier to predict R from the other features. If it predicts well, the data is not MCAR.
  • MAR and MNAR cannot be told apart from the data alone. Distinguishing them requires domain knowledge.

⚠️ Gotcha: Missingness can itself be a signal. Add a binary missing indicator feature, especially when MNAR is suspected. Tree models (XGBoost, LightGBM) learn a default split direction for missing values natively.

2.2 Imputation Techniques

Mean / Median / Mode

  • Pros: Fast, simple, deterministic.
  • Cons:
    • Shrinks variance, which narrows CIs artificially
    • Weakens correlations between features
    • Distorts the distribution (creates a spike at the imputed value)
  • When to use: Low missingness (under ~5%), MCAR data, baselines. Prefer the median for skewed data and the mode for categoricals.

KNN imputation

Fills a missing value with the (distance-weighted) average of the k nearest neighbours, measured on the observed features.

  • Pros: Captures local, non-linear structure. Works for mixed patterns.
  • Cons:
    • O(n²) cost
    • Requires scaling
    • Degrades in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality)
    • Sensitive to the choice of k
  • When to use: Moderate data sizes, MAR data, features with meaningful similarity structure.

MICE (Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations)

Algorithm:

  1. Fill all missing values with simple placeholders (e.g., the mean).
  2. For each variable that has missing values, regress it on all other variables and impute from the predictive distribution (adding noise, not just the point prediction).
  3. Cycle through all variables for several iterations until values converge.
  4. Repeat the whole process to create m complete datasets (typically 5–20).
  5. Fit the analysis model on each dataset and pool the results using Rubin's Rules.

Rubin's Rules (Q̂ᵢ is the estimate from dataset i, Uᵢ its within-dataset variance):

The total variance T reflects uncertainty from the imputation itself. This is the main advantage of MICE over single imputation.

pythonfrom sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer, KNNImputer, SimpleImputer

mice = IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, sample_posterior=True, random_state=0)
# sample_posterior=True + different random_state → multiple imputations
Scenario Recommended
MCAR, under 5% missing, baseline Mean/median + missing indicator
MAR, need valid statistical inference MICE (multiple imputation)
MAR, non-linear local structure, mid-size data KNN
Prediction-only with GBMs Native NaN handling + missing indicator
MNAR Domain modeling + sensitivity analysis. Flag as a limitation

⚠️ Gotcha: sklearn's IterativeImputer returns a single imputation by default. Real MICE needs m runs and pooled results. Always fit imputers on the training fold only, inside a Pipeline.

2.3 Feature Scaling

Scaler Formula Output Outlier-robust? Use when
StandardScaler Mean 0, std 1 No Linear/logistic regression, SVM, PCA, neural networks
MinMaxScaler [0, 1] No (very sensitive) Bounded inputs (images, neural networks with sigmoid)
RobustScaler Median 0 Yes Data with heavy outliers

Who needs scaling:

  • Distance-based models: KNN, K-Means, SVM (RBF kernel)
  • Gradient-descent optimizers: scaling improves convergence
  • Regularized models: the penalty depends on coefficient magnitude
  • PCA: variance-driven
  • Tree-based models do not need scaling. Splits are invariant to monotonic transforms.

⚠️ Gotchas

  • "Normalization" is ambiguous. It can mean min-max scaling or L2 row normalization (Normalizer). Clarify which one you mean.
  • StandardScaler does not make data normal. It only shifts and rescales. To reduce skew, use a log, Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson transform (PowerTransformer).
  • Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting is leakage.

2.4 Encoding Categorical Variables

One-Hot Encoding

  • Creates one binary column per category.
  • Dummy variable trap: In unregularized linear models with an intercept, one column is perfectly collinear with the others. Use drop='first'.
  • Cons:
    • Dimensionality explodes for high-cardinality features
    • Produces sparse matrices
    • Fragments tree splits
  • Unseen categories at inference: set handle_unknown='ignore'.

Ordinal Encoding

  • Maps categories to integers (e.g., Low=0, Medium=1, High=2).
  • Correct only when a true order exists.
  • Applied to nominal categories, it introduces a fake order into linear models. Trees often tolerate it.

Target (Mean) Encoding

Replaces each category with the target mean for that category, smoothed toward the global mean:

  • is the category count and m the smoothing strength.
  • Rare categories shrink toward the global prior.

Leakage risk: If you encode each row using its own target value, the model memorizes the target. This is especially bad for rare categories, where the encoding nearly equals y.

Fixes:

  1. Out-of-fold (K-fold) encoding: Encode each training row using statistics from the other folds.
  2. Smoothing / additive noise.
  3. CatBoost ordered target statistics: Encode using only the rows that come earlier in a random ordering.
  4. Note on sklearn's TargetEncoder (≥1.3): fit_transform uses internal cross-fitting, but fit().transform() on the training data does not. This difference is a common interview trap.
Encoding Cardinality Model type Leakage risk
One-Hot Low (under ~20) Linear, neural networks None
Ordinal Any (if ordered) Trees, ordered features None
Target High GBMs, linear High unless out-of-fold
Frequency / Hashing Very high Any Low

2.5 Outlier Detection & Handling

IQR rule (Tukey fences):

Works without a distributional assumption and is robust. It is univariate only.

Z-score: Flag a point if . This assumes approximate normality.

Masking problem: Extreme outliers inflate σ, which hides other outliers. The robust fix is the Modified Z-score based on the median absolute deviation (MAD):

Isolation Forest

  • Idea: Anomalies are few and different, so random partitioning isolates them in fewer splits (shorter path lengths).
  • Anomaly score:

where (Euler's constant).

  • Interpreting the score: s → 1 means anomalous; s ≪ 0.5 means normal.
  • Pros: Multivariate, roughly O(n log n), no distance computations, scales well.
  • Cons: The contamination parameter must be guessed. It struggles with local anomalies in clusters of varying density (LOF handles those better).

Handling strategies:

  1. Investigate first. Is it a data error or a genuine extreme? (Fraud is the outlier you want to find.)
  2. Correct or remove clear data-entry errors.
  3. Cap / winsorize (e.g., at the 1st and 99th percentiles, computed on training data only).
  4. Transform (log, Box-Cox).
  5. Use robust methods: Huber loss, quantile regression, tree models, median-based statistics.

⚠️ Gotcha: Removing outliers before the train/test split, based on statistics from the full data, is leakage. Removing them from the test set inflates offline metrics, because production data will contain them.

SECTION 3: CORE MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS

3.1 Linear Regression

Model:

Cost (MSE):

Closed-form OLS solution:

The closed form costs O(np² + p³). Use gradient descent at very large scale.

Assumptions (LINE + no multicollinearity):

Assumption Diagnostic Violation remedy
Linearity (in parameters) Residuals vs. fitted plot Transformations, polynomial/spline terms
Independence of errors Durbin-Watson, ACF of residuals Time series models, clustered SEs
Normality of errors Q-Q plot, Shapiro-Wilk Only needed for small-sample inference. Bootstrap
Equal variance (homoscedasticity) Breusch-Pagan, residual funnel WLS, log-transform y, robust (HC) SEs
No perfect multicollinearity VIF: (VIF above 5–10 is a concern) Drop or combine features, Ridge, PCA

Gauss–Markov theorem: Under linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity and no autocorrelation, OLS is BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator). Normality is not required for BLUE.

3.2 Logistic Regression

Model:

Cost (Binary Cross-Entropy / Log-Loss). This is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli distribution and is convex:

Gradient:

There is no closed-form solution. Fit with Newton-Raphson/IRLS, L-BFGS or SGD.

Interpretation: A one-unit increase in multiplies the odds by .

⚠️ Gotchas

  • Why not use MSE for logistic regression? Combined with the sigmoid, MSE produces a non-convex loss and weak gradients when predictions are confidently wrong.
  • Perfect separation: If the classes are perfectly separable, coefficients diverge to ±∞. Regularization fixes this.
  • Logistic regression is a linear classifier: the decision boundary is linear in feature space.

3.3 Regularization

Penalty Effect Closed form?
Ridge (L2) Shrinks all coefficients smoothly. Handles multicollinearity Yes
Lasso (L1) Sparsity (feature selection) No (coordinate descent)
ElasticNet Sparsity + grouping of correlated features No

Why L1 produces sparsity:

  • Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond (cross-polytope). Its corners lie on the axes, so the loss contours tend to touch it at a corner, where some coefficients are exactly zero.
  • The L2 constraint region is a sphere, with no corners.

Bayesian view:

  • Ridge is the MAP estimate under a Gaussian prior.
  • Lasso is the MAP estimate under a Laplace prior.

⚠️ Gotchas

  • Always standardize before regularizing. Otherwise the penalty depends on the feature's units.
  • Do not penalize the intercept.
  • With correlated features, Lasso arbitrarily picks one and is unstable across samples. ElasticNet spreads weight across the group.
  • Lasso selects at most n features when p > n. ElasticNet does not have this limit.
  • Tune λ by cross-validation. The "1-SE rule" gives a sparser model.

3.4 Decision Trees

Greedy recursive partitioning. At each node, choose the split that maximizes the impurity decrease.

Gini impurity:

Entropy:

Information gain:

Regression trees split to minimize variance (MSE) within the child nodes.

Gini vs. Entropy:

  • They produce nearly the same splits (they differ in only about 2% of cases empirically).
  • Gini is slightly faster because it needs no logarithm. It is the CART default.
  • Entropy penalizes impure nodes a bit more and tends toward more balanced trees.
  • Max Gini for binary classes is 0.5. Max entropy is 1.0.

Pros:

  • Interpretable
  • No scaling needed
  • Handles non-linearity and interactions
  • Mixed data types

Cons:

  • High variance: small data changes produce a very different tree
  • Overfits without pruning (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, cost-complexity pruning via ccp_alpha)
  • Piecewise-constant boundaries aligned with the axes
  • Cannot extrapolate

3.5 Random Forest (Bagging)

Method:

  • Train B trees, each on a bootstrap sample (about 63.2% unique rows).
  • Consider only a random subset of features at each split:
    • classification:
    • regression:
  • Average the predictions (regression) or take a majority vote (classification).

Why it works. For B trees, each with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the ensemble variance is:

Bagging reduces the second term. Feature subsampling reduces ρ, which is what separates Random Forest from plain bagged trees.

  • Out-of-Bag (OOB) error: Each tree is evaluated on the ~36.8% of rows it never saw. This gives a free validation estimate.
  • Pros: Robust, little tuning, parallelizable, reduces variance.
  • Cons: Does not reduce bias, large models, slow inference, cannot extrapolate.

3.6 Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM (Boosting)

Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially. Each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss (the pseudo-residuals):

ν is the learning rate (shrinkage). With MSE loss, the pseudo-residuals are just the ordinary residuals. Boosting mainly reduces bias.

XGBoost uses a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss and an explicit regularization term:

Optimal leaf weight ( and are the sums of gradients and Hessians in leaf j):

Split gain:

Other XGBoost features:

  • Sparsity-aware split finding (learns a default direction for missing values)
  • Column subsampling
  • Parallel split finding

LightGBM:

  • Histogram-based splits (bins continuous features)
  • Leaf-wise growth (best-first), which is more accurate but overfits more easily. Control it with num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf.
  • GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling): keeps high-gradient rows and samples low-gradient rows
  • EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling): merges sparse, mutually exclusive features
  • Very fast on large data

CatBoost (worth mentioning): ordered boosting and ordered target statistics handle categoricals without leakage.

Random Forest GBM / XGBoost / LightGBM
Ensemble type Parallel (bagging) Sequential (boosting)
Reduces Variance Bias (and variance through shrinkage)
Tree depth Deep, fully grown Shallow (3–8 levels)
Overfitting risk Low as trees are added High if there are too many rounds. Use early stopping
Tuning effort Low High (learning rate, n_estimators, depth, subsample, regularization)

⚠️ Gotchas

  • Impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features. Use permutation importance or SHAP.
  • In boosting, the learning rate and number of trees trade off against each other. Lower the learning rate, add trees, and use early stopping on a validation set.
  • Leaf-wise vs. level-wise: A LightGBM tree with num_leaves=2^max_depth is far more complex than an XGBoost depth-wise tree of the same depth.

3.7 K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)

Method:

  • A non-parametric, lazy learner: there is no training step.
  • Prediction is the majority vote or mean of the k nearest training points.
  • Common distances:
    • Euclidean:
    • Manhattan
    • Minkowski
    • Cosine (for text and embeddings)

Effect of k:

  • Small k gives low bias and high variance (noisy boundaries).
  • Large k gives high bias and smooth boundaries.
  • Use an odd k for binary problems to avoid ties.

Pros: Simple, no training, naturally multi-class.

Cons:

  • O(n) prediction cost per query (use KD-trees, Ball trees or approximate nearest neighbours)
  • Requires scaling
  • Curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions, all points become roughly equidistant

3.8 K-Means Clustering

Objective. Minimize the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS, or inertia):

Lloyd's algorithm:

  1. Initialize the centroids. Use k-means++, which spreads the initial centroids out.
  2. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
  3. Recompute each centroid as the mean of its points.
  4. Repeat until assignments stop changing. This converges to a local optimum, so use multiple restarts (n_init).

Elbow method: Plot WCSS against k and choose the "elbow" where the gains flatten out. This is subjective.

Silhouette score for point i:

  • a(i) is the mean distance to points in the same cluster.
  • b(i) is the mean distance to the nearest other cluster.
  • Choose the k that maximizes the mean silhouette. Scores near 1 mean well separated; near 0 means overlapping; negative means likely misassigned.

Assumptions and limitations:

  • Assumes spherical, similar-size, similar-density clusters
  • Sensitive to outliers and scaling
  • You must pick k in advance
  • Euclidean distance only (the mean minimizes squared Euclidean distance)

Alternatives:

  • DBSCAN: arbitrary shapes, finds noise points
  • GMM: soft assignments, elliptical clusters
  • Hierarchical clustering
  • K-Medoids: robust to outliers

3.9 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Goal: Find orthogonal directions of maximum variance.

Steps:

  1. Center the data (and usually standardize it).
  2. Compute the covariance matrix:
  3. Eigendecompose it:

Interpretation:

  • Eigenvectors are the principal directions (loadings).
  • Eigenvalues are the variance captured along each direction.

Explained variance ratio:

Keep enough components to reach a cumulative EVR threshold (e.g., 90–95%), or use the scree plot elbow.

SVD link: If , then the principal directions are the columns of V, and . In practice PCA is computed via SVD because it is numerically more stable.

Pros:

  • Removes multicollinearity
  • Denoises
  • Compresses data
  • Supports visualization

Cons:

  • Linear only (use Kernel PCA, UMAP or t-SNE for non-linear structure)
  • Components are hard to interpret
  • Sensitive to scaling and outliers

⚠️ Gotchas

  • PCA is unsupervised. A low-variance component can be the most predictive one for the target. If supervision matters, consider PLS.
  • Forgetting to standardize lets features with large units dominate the components.
  • Fit PCA on the training data only.

3.10 Evaluation Metrics

Confusion matrix:

Predicted + Predicted −
Actual + TP FN
Actual − FP TN

Precision, recall and F1:

F-beta (β > 1 weights recall more heavily):

ROC-AUC:

  • The area under the TPR vs. FPR curve across all thresholds, where
  • Probabilistic meaning: the probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked above a randomly chosen negative.
  • A random model scores 0.5.

PR-AUC (Average Precision): Preferred under severe imbalance. ROC can look excellent there because FPR is diluted by the large number of true negatives.

Log-Loss: Measures the quality and calibration of the probabilities. It heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions.

Regression metrics:

Metric Use when Watch out
Accuracy Balanced classes, equal error costs Misleading with imbalance (99% accuracy by always predicting the majority class)
Precision False positives are costly (spam filter, fraud alerts sent to analysts) Ignores false negatives
Recall False negatives are costly (cancer screening, fraud loss) Ignores false positives
F1 You need a balance and positives are rare Ignores TN. Threshold-dependent
ROC-AUC Ranking quality, balanced-ish classes Insensitive to calibration. Optimistic under imbalance
PR-AUC Severe imbalance Baseline equals the prevalence, not 0.5
Log-Loss Probabilities are used directly (bidding, risk scoring) Unbounded. Sensitive to overconfidence
MSE / RMSE Large errors are disproportionately bad. RMSE is in the units of y Sensitive to outliers
MAE Robust, interpretable average error Gradient not smooth at 0
MAPE Scale-free reporting to the business Undefined at y = 0, explodes near 0, penalizes over-forecasts more heavily (asymmetric). Use WAPE or sMAPE instead

⚠️ Gotchas

  • MSE is minimized by the conditional mean. MAE is minimized by the conditional median. Choose based on what the business needs.
  • AUC can be high while probabilities are badly calibrated. Check with a reliability diagram, Brier score, or Platt/isotonic calibration.
  • Precision and recall depend on the threshold. Pick the threshold from the business cost matrix, not the default 0.5.

SECTION 4: END-TO-END TIME SERIES ANALYSIS

4.1 Core Concepts

Decomposition:

  • Additive:
  • Multiplicative: . Take logs to convert to additive. Use this form when seasonal amplitude grows with the level.

Components:

  • Trend (T): Long-run direction.
  • Seasonality (S): A fixed, known period (daily, weekly, yearly).
  • Cyclicality (C): Fluctuations without a fixed period, typically longer than a year (business and economic cycles). Interviewers frequently test the difference between cyclicality and seasonality.
  • Noise (ε): The remaining irregular component.

Use STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) for robust decomposition.

Weak (covariance) stationarity requires:

  1. A constant mean:
  2. A constant variance:
  3. Autocovariance that depends only on the lag:

ARMA-type models require stationarity because their parameters must be constant over time.

Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test:

  • H₀: γ = 0 (unit root, non-stationary).
  • H₁: γ < 0 (stationary).
  • p < 0.05 means reject H₀, so the series is stationary.

KPSS test has the opposite null hypothesis (H₀: stationary). Use both:

  • ADF rejects + KPSS fails to reject → stationary
  • ADF fails to reject + KPSS rejects → unit root, so difference the series
  • Results conflict → trend-stationary or difference-stationary ambiguity

Making a series stationary:

  • Differencing:
  • Seasonal differencing:
  • Log or Box-Cox transforms (stabilize variance)
  • Detrending

4.2 Traditional Models

AR(p): Regression on its own past values.

MA(q): Regression on past forecast errors (shocks).

ARMA(p, q): Combines both, for stationary series.

ARIMA(p, d, q): ARMA applied after differencing d times. Using the backshift operator B:

SARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)ₛ: Adds seasonal AR/MA/differencing at period s:

SARIMAX adds exogenous regressors.

Reading ACF and PACF plots

  • ACF (autocorrelation function): the total correlation at lag k.
  • PACF (partial autocorrelation function): the correlation at lag k after removing the effect of the intermediate lags.
Pattern ACF PACF Model
AR(p) Tails off (exponential or sinusoidal decay) Cuts off after lag p AR(p)
MA(q) Cuts off after lag q Tails off MA(q)
ARMA(p, q) Tails off Tails off ARMA. Choose order by AIC/BIC
Non-stationary Decays very slowly, stays high Large spike at lag 1 Difference first
Seasonal Spikes at s, 2s, 3s… Spikes at s, 2s… Add seasonal P/Q terms

Model selection and diagnostics:

  • Compare models with AIC/BIC, or use auto_arima.
  • Residuals should be white noise. Check with the Ljung-Box test (p > 0.05 means no remaining autocorrelation).
pythonfrom statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

adf_stat, p_value, *_ = adfuller(y)
print(f"ADF p-value: {p_value:.4f}")  # < 0.05 → stationary

plot_acf(y.diff().dropna(), lags=40); plot_pacf(y.diff().dropna(), lags=40)

model = SARIMAX(y, order=(1,1,1), seasonal_order=(1,1,1,12)).fit(disp=False)
print(model.summary())
forecast = model.get_forecast(steps=12).summary_frame()  # includes CI

⚠️ Gotcha: Over-differencing introduces artificial negative autocorrelation (an ACF spike near −0.5 at lag 1). If differencing twice still looks non-stationary, suspect a structural break.

4.3 Advanced Time Series

Prophet (Meta) is a decomposable additive regression model, not an autoregressive one:

  • g(t): Piecewise-linear or logistic trend with automatic changepoints (sparse prior on rate changes).
  • s(t): Fourier-series seasonality:
  • h(t): Holiday or event effects.
  • Pros:
    • Handles missing data and outliers
    • Supports multiple seasonalities
    • Interpretable, quick for business analysts
  • Cons:
    • Does not use autoregressive structure, so it often underperforms on short-horizon forecasts with strong autocorrelation
    • Weak on data without strong seasonality
    • Can overfit changepoints

NeuralProphet:

  • Built on PyTorch. Keeps Prophet's components and adds AR-Net (neural autoregression), lagged and future regressors, and optional hidden layers.
  • Pros: Captures local autocorrelation, so it is often better at short horizons.
  • Cons: More hyperparameters, slower training, less mature.

Turning time series into a supervised ML problem

Reframe the problem as predicting from features available at time t − 1:

pythonimport pandas as pd

def make_features(df, target='sales'):
    df = df.sort_values('date').copy()
    # Lag features
    for lag in [1, 7, 14, 28]:
        df[f'lag_{lag}'] = df[target].shift(lag)
    # Rolling windows — SHIFT FIRST to avoid using y_t itself
    for w in [7, 28]:
        df[f'roll_mean_{w}'] = df[target].shift(1).rolling(w).mean()
        df[f'roll_std_{w}']  = df[target].shift(1).rolling(w).std()
    # Expanding / EWM
    df['ewm_7'] = df[target].shift(1).ewm(span=7).mean()
    # Calendar features
    df['dow'] = df['date'].dt.dayofweek
    df['month'] = df['date'].dt.month
    df['is_month_end'] = df['date'].dt.is_month_end.astype(int)
    return df.dropna()

Multi-step forecasting strategies:

Strategy How Trade-off
Recursive A single 1-step model whose predictions feed back as lags Errors accumulate
Direct A separate model for each horizon h No error accumulation, but H models to train
MIMO / multi-output One model outputs the whole horizon vector Captures dependencies between horizons

Pros of ML (GBMs) over ARIMA:

  • Handles many series at once (global models)
  • Uses exogenous features
  • Captures non-linearity

Cons:

  • Cannot extrapolate trends (trees). Detrend or difference the target first.
  • Needs careful feature engineering.

4.4 Validation: Walk-Forward with TimeSeriesSplit

Never use random K-Fold on time series. It trains on the future to predict the past.

textFold 1: [Train ████]          [Test ██]
Fold 2: [Train ██████]        [Test ██]
Fold 3: [Train ████████]      [Test ██]
Fold 4: [Train ██████████]    [Test ██]

pythonimport numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=28, gap=7)  # gap = purge buffer
scores = []
for tr_idx, te_idx in tscv.split(X):
    X_tr, X_te = X.iloc[tr_idx], X.iloc[te_idx]
    y_tr, y_te = y.iloc[tr_idx], y.iloc[te_idx]
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    scores.append(mean_absolute_error(y_te, model.predict(X_te)))
print(f"MAE: {np.mean(scores):.2f} ± {np.std(scores):.2f}")

Split variations:

  • Expanding window: The default. Use all history up to each cutoff.
  • Sliding window: Use a fixed-length training window (max_train_size). Better when the data has regime changes or concept drift.
  • Gap / purging: Leave a buffer between train and test, so features built from overlapping windows (e.g., a 7-day rolling target) do not leak across the boundary.

⚠️ Gotchas (temporal leakage)

  • Rolling features without .shift(1) include the current target.
  • Fitting scalers or imputers on the full series before splitting.
  • Using future-known information as features (e.g., "final monthly total" during the month).
  • In panel or multi-series data, split by time, not by series ID alone.
  • Backtest horizons must match the production forecast horizon and the production data-availability lag.

SECTION 5: MOCK INTERVIEW CHEATSHEET & TRAPS

5.1 Bias-Variance Tradeoff

For a technical interviewer

For squared error loss, with and :

  • Bias: Error from wrong assumptions. The model is too simple and underfits (e.g., a linear model on a non-linear relationship).
  • Variance: Sensitivity to the particular training sample. The model is too flexible and overfits (e.g., a deep unpruned tree).
  • Levers that move along the tradeoff:
    • Model complexity
    • Regularization strength (λ)
    • Tree depth
    • k in KNN
    • Number of boosting rounds
    • Amount of training data (more data reduces variance)
  • Ensembles:
    • Bagging (Random Forest) reduces variance.
    • Boosting reduces bias.
  • Diagnosis:
    • High training error and high validation error → bias.
    • Low training error and high validation error → variance.
    • Use learning curves.
  • Senior-level nuance: Modern overparameterized models (deep nets) show double descent: test error can fall again beyond the interpolation threshold. The classical U-curve is not universal.

For a non-technical stakeholder

"Think of two new analysts forecasting next quarter's sales. The first uses one rule: 'sales grow 5% every quarter.' He's consistent but always misses the big shifts. That's bias: too simple. The second memorizes every detail of last year, including one-off events like a warehouse fire. She nails last year perfectly but gets confused by anything new. That's variance: too sensitive to the past. We want a model in between, one that learns the real patterns and ignores the noise. We check this by testing the model on data it has never seen."

5.2 Handling Severe Class Imbalance (e.g., 1:1000)

Work through these steps in order, which is the structured answer senior interviewers look for.

Step 1: Fix the metric first.

  • Accuracy is meaningless here.
  • Use PR-AUC, recall at a fixed precision (or the reverse), F-beta, or expected business cost.
  • Use stratified splits so every fold contains positives.

Step 2: Algorithm-level fixes (preferred: no synthetic data).

  • Class weights. Scale the loss contribution by inverse class frequency: . In sklearn use class_weight='balanced'. In XGBoost use scale_pos_weight = n_neg / n_pos.
  • Focal loss. Down-weights easy, well-classified examples so training focuses on hard ones:
  • Focal loss details:
    • is the model's probability for the true class.
    • γ (typically 2) controls how strongly easy examples are suppressed.
    • With γ = 0, focal loss reduces to weighted cross-entropy.
    • Originally from object detection (RetinaNet). Useful in deep learning and GBMs with custom objectives.

Step 3: Data-level fixes.

  • Random undersampling of the majority class. Fast, but discards information.
  • Random oversampling of the minority class. Risks overfitting to duplicated rows.
  • SMOTE: Synthesizes minority points by interpolating between a minority point and one of its k minority-class neighbours:
  • SMOTE cons:
    • Creates noise near the class boundary
    • Poor in high dimensions
    • Invalid for categorical features (use SMOTENC)
  • SMOTE variants: Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN.

Step 4: Decision-level fixes.

  • Tune the threshold on a validation set using the cost matrix. This is often the highest-ROI step.
  • Recalibrate probabilities after resampling or reweighting, because predicted probabilities become biased toward the minority class. Correct for the prior shift, or use isotonic or Platt calibration.

Step 5: Reframe the problem if appropriate: anomaly detection (Isolation Forest, autoencoders), or collecting more positive examples.

pythonfrom imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline   # NOT sklearn's — supports samplers
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score

pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()),
                 ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=0)),
                 ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print(cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='average_precision').mean())

⚠️ Gotchas

  • Applying SMOTE before the train/test split (or before CV) is leakage. Synthetic points derived from test rows end up in training. Resample only inside the training fold.
  • Never resample the test set. It must reflect the real-world class distribution.
  • With modern GBMs, class weights plus threshold tuning usually match or beat SMOTE.

5.3 Data Leakage

Definition: Information that would not be available at prediction time reaches the model during training or evaluation. Offline metrics are inflated, and the model then fails in production.

Two types:

  • Target leakage: A feature encodes the label.
  • Train-test contamination: Information from the evaluation data influences training.

Three subtle ways leakage happens during data preparation

1. Fitting preprocessing on the full dataset before splitting or CV

  • Scalers, imputers, PCA, outlier caps and especially feature selection (e.g., choosing the top-k features by correlation with y on all data) all learn test-set statistics.
  • Feature selection on the full data is particularly bad. It can produce high CV scores on pure noise.
  • Fix: Put every fitted step inside a Pipeline so it is refit within each fold.

2. Target encoding or aggregates computed with the row's own target

  • Category mean encodings, "customer historical conversion rate" or group averages that include the current row (or future rows) leak the label. Rare categories are the worst affected.
  • Fix: Out-of-fold encoding, ordered target statistics, or point-in-time aggregates that use only past data.

3. Temporal and group leakage hidden by random splits

  • Temporal: Random K-Fold on time-ordered data. Rolling features without a shift. Features whose values were updated after the event (e.g., "account_status = closed" used to predict churn, or "days_since_last_payment" recomputed after the default).
  • Group: The same patient, user or device appears in both train and test (duplicate or near-duplicate rows, multiple images per patient). The model memorizes the entity instead of learning the pattern.
  • Fix: Use TimeSeriesSplit or a point-in-time feature store with "as-of" joins. Use GroupKFold or StratifiedGroupKFold. Deduplicate before splitting.

Other examples worth mentioning:

  • Proxy features generated downstream of the label (e.g., "refund_issued" when predicting fraud)
  • Resampling (SMOTE) before the split
  • Hyperparameter tuning on the test set (use nested CV or a held-out set)

Red flags in an interview:

  • Suspiciously high performance (e.g., AUC above 0.99 on a hard problem)
  • A single dominant feature in importance plots
  • A large gap between offline and online metrics
python# Leak-proof pattern: every fitted transform lives inside the CV loop
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler, TargetEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_score

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', Pipeline([('imp', SimpleImputer(strategy='median', add_indicator=True)),
                      ('sc', StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ('low_card', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), low_card_cols),
    ('high_card', TargetEncoder(), high_card_cols),   # cross-fitted in fit_transform
])
pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('model', clf)])
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, groups=customer_id,
                         cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=5), scoring='roc_auc')

Quick Revision Table: The 15 Most Common Interview Traps

# Trap question Correct core answer
1 "What does a p-value of 0.03 mean?" P(data this extreme | H₀), not P(H₀ true)
2 "95% CI means 95% chance the parameter is inside?" No. 95% of such intervals would contain it
3 "Stopped the A/B test early because it was significant" Peeking inflates Type I error. Use sequential testing
4 "Mean-impute everything?" Shrinks variance and correlations. Check MCAR/MAR/MNAR
5 "Scale features for Random Forest?" Not needed. Trees are invariant to monotonic transforms
6 "Why does Lasso give zeros?" L1 constraint has corners on the axes
7 "Why not MSE for logistic regression?" Non-convex with sigmoid. Log-loss is the Bernoulli MLE
8 "RF vs. GBM?" Bagging reduces variance. Boosting reduces bias
9 "Trust impurity feature importance?" Biased toward high cardinality. Use permutation/SHAP
10 "Always standardize before PCA?" Yes, when units differ. PCA is variance-driven
11 "99% accuracy on fraud: good?" Meaningless under imbalance. Use PR-AUC
12 "MAPE for demand with zero-sales days?" Undefined/explodes. Use WAPE or MASE
13 "ADF p = 0.30, so stationary?" No. You fail to reject the unit root, so it is non-stationary
14 "K-Fold on time series?" Leaks the future. Use walk-forward TimeSeriesSplit
15 "SMOTE then split?" Leakage. Resample inside the training fold only
